## Summary

| | |
|---|---|
| **Contributor** | Srishti Dutta ([\@srishtiii28](https://github.com/srishtiii28)) |
| **Organization** | The R Project for Statistical Computing |
| **Mentor** | Christophe Regouby ([\@cregouby](https://github.com/cregouby)) |
| **Repositories** | [mlverse/torchvision](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision), [mlverse/torchvisionlib](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvisionlib) |

The work spans two packages. In **torchvision**, an R port of PyTorch's vision
library, I added the LW-DETR family of real-time detection transformers and
built out the `item_transform_*` family, which are augmentations that transform
a whole dataset item so the image and its target (bounding boxes or
segmentation masks) stay aligned. In **torchvisionlib**, which supplies compiled
ops to torchvision, I contributed two native operators: the multi-scale
deformable attention kernel that LW-DETR's decoder depends on, and rotated-box
IoU.

---

## Merged pull requests

### 1. Fix `draw_keypoints()` documentation and error message typo

[mlverse/torchvision#296](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/296) ·
merged 25 March 2026 · +19 -7 across 3 files

My first contribution to the package. Three documentation defects in
`R/vision_utils.R`. The `connectivity` parameter was annotated as a `Vector`
when it accepts a `list(c(i, j), ...)` of pairs, and carried a stale
"currently unavailable" note describing behaviour that had since been
implemented. The `colors` parameter had two copy-paste errors carried over from
`draw_bounding_boxes()`: it said `"boxes"` where it meant `"keypoints"`, twice,
and named `"viridis"` when the function calls `grDevices::rainbow()`. An error
message read `"but is current shape is"`. All three were fixed at the roxygen2
source with `man/draw_keypoints.Rd` regenerated, which is the part I had to be
told about.

### 2. Dispatch NMS to `torchvisionlib::ops_nms()` when available

[mlverse/torchvision#325](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/325) ·
merged 10 June 2026 · +45 -4 across 4 files ·
closes [#321](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/321),
[#322](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/322)

Non-maximum suppression ran in pure R on every inference call for all four
FasterRCNN variants and both MaskRCNN variants, and it dominated their runtime.
`nms()` now dispatches to the native C++ `torchvisionlib::ops_nms()` when
torchvisionlib is installed, and keeps the pure R path as a fallback so
behaviour is unchanged for users without it.

Measured on a 520×520 image on CPU:

| Model | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| `model_fasterrcnn_mobilenet_v3_large_320_fpn` | ~25 s / image | ~2 s / image |
| `model_maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn` | ~1.7 min / image | ~25 s / image |

FasterRCNN went from unusable for interactive work to responsive. Tests cover
both the native dispatch and the fallback, since the point of the change is
that the two agree.

### 3. Add LW-DETR object detection models

[mlverse/torchvision#334](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/334) ·
merged 4 July 2026 · +1,419 -6 across 13 files ·
closes [#328](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/328)

An implementation of [LW-DETR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03459), a real-time
detection transformer, in a single 1,101-line `R/models-lw_detr.R`. The
architecture has three stages.

The **ViT backbone** interleaves windowed and global attention. Which blocks
are windowed is set per variant by `window_block_indexes`, and intermediate
activations are tapped at `out_feature_indexes` rather than only at the final
layer, so the projector receives several depths of feature at once.

The **C2f projector** takes those tapped features and produces the multi-scale
feature map the decoder samples from. On the large variant it runs at two
scales, `c(2.0, 0.5)`, which is why that variant carries its own sampling and
scale layers.

The **two-stage decoder** generates proposals from the feature map, then refines
them with deformable cross-attention over a small number of sampled points per
query (`n_points`, 2 on the smaller variants and 4 on large) instead of
attending to every spatial position.

Four variants are exposed:

| | `embed_dim` | depth | queries | scales | `n_points` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| `model_lw_detr_tiny()` | 192 | 6 | 100 | 1.0 | 2 |
| `model_lw_detr_small()` | 192 | 10 | 300 | 1.0 | 2 |
| `model_lw_detr_medium()` | 384 | 10 | 300 | 1.0 | 2 |
| `model_lw_detr_large()` | 384 | 10 | 300 | 2.0, 0.5 | 4 |

All four load the official COCO checkpoints with exact key and shape match and
reproduce reference detections. Getting there was most of the work: a port that
runs is easy to write and hard to trust, and matching keys against the reference
implementation is what turns "it produces boxes" into "it produces the right
boxes".

`forward()` takes `(images, pixel_mask = NULL)`. Non-square inputs are handled
by letterboxing, resizing the longest side to 640 and padding to 640×640, then
passing a logical `pixel_mask` that is `TRUE` over real pixels. The padded
region is excluded from attention and boxes come back in the coordinates of the
unpadded image, which matches the reference preprocessing. Omitting the mask
treats the whole frame as valid and is only correct for square, unpadded input.

The decoder's cross-attention needs multi-scale deformable attention. At this
point only a pure R `nnf_grid_sample()` fallback existed, which is what led to
the CUDA op in contribution 5 below.

This replaced an earlier attempt in
[#332](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/332), which I closed and
rewrote after review.

### 4. Preallocate lists and vectors before iteration loops

[mlverse/torchvision#341](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/341) ·
merged 20 July 2026 · +154 -170 across 15 files ·
closes [#335](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/335)

A package-wide cleanup, and the only contribution that removed more lines than
it added. Lists grown one element at a time reallocate on every iteration, so
where the final length is known before the loop they are now allocated with
`vector("list", n)` and assigned by index. `folder_make_dataset()` and the
Cityscapes image collection gather into a preallocated list and `unlist()` once
instead of calling `c()` per iteration, which is the case where the old pattern
cost the most, since those loops run over every file in a dataset directory.
Touches fifteen model and dataset files.

### 5. Multi-scale deformable attention CUDA op

[mlverse/torchvisionlib#33](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvisionlib/pull/33) ·
merged 1 August 2026 · +2,136 -29 across 26 files ·
fixes [#25](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvisionlib/issues/25)

The largest contribution of the summer, and the one that took the longest.
`ops_ms_deform_attn()` is the operator LW-DETR's decoder cross-attention needs,
replacing the pure R `grid_sample` fallback on GPU.

The op itself is only part of it. Adding a native operator to torchvisionlib
means writing the CUDA kernel and its `im2col` helper, a CPU kernel, and the
autograd binding, then threading the symbol through the export plumbing on both
the `csrc/` and `src/` sides, the `.def` export files, and the Rcpp bindings,
before it is callable from R at all. The R-CMD-check workflow needed updating
too. That is why a single operator touches 26 files.

The signature is
`ops_ms_deform_attn(value, spatial_shapes, level_start_index, sampling_locations, attention_weights, im2col_step = 64)`.
One detail worth recording, because it cost me time: `spatial_shapes` and
`level_start_index` keep the kernel's 0-based indexing convention rather than
being converted to R's 1-based indexing. The output is a feature tensor rather
than a set of indices, so no adjustment is applied on the way back either. This
is the opposite of the convention in `ops_nms()`, which does `$add(1L)` on its
result precisely because it returns indices. Both are documented now.

### 6. `item_transform_affine()` and `target_transform_affine()`

[mlverse/torchvision#367](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/367) ·
merged 10 August 2026 · +684 across 15 files ·
closes [#347](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/347)

Applies an affine transformation, meaning rotation, translation, scale and
shear, to a whole dataset item so the target stays aligned with the image.

This is where I learned the S3 pattern the rest of my summer's work follows.
A generic dispatches on the item's class, so
`item_transform_affine.image_with_bounding_box()` warps boxes,
`item_transform_affine.image_with_segmentation_mask()` warps masks, and
`item_transform_affine.dataset()` wraps `.getitem()` so the same transform
applies to every item a dataset yields. A `.default()` method exists only to
raise a clear error when the input is a bare tensor rather than an item, which
is the mistake a user is most likely to make.

The split between `item_transform_*` and `target_transform_*` matters: the
target transform does the geometry on boxes alone and is reusable, while the
item transform is the layer that keeps image and target consistent. The
convention comes from
[#343](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/343), the umbrella issue
tracking `item_transform_` coverage against PyTorch's `transforms.v2`.

### 7. Extend `item_transform_rotate()` to segmentation

[mlverse/torchvision#379](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/379) ·
merged 10 August 2026 · +115 -10 across 5 files ·
closes [#363](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/363)

Adds `item_transform_rotate.image_with_segmentation_mask()` and
`item_transform_rotate.dataset()`.

The mask branch rotates the image with whatever `interpolation` and `fill` the
caller passed, but always rotates the masks with `interpolation = 0` and
`fill = 0`. Masks hold discrete class labels, so bilinear resampling would
average neighbouring labels into values that are not classes at all. It also
updates `image_height` and `image_width` on the target, because `expand = TRUE`
grows the canvas and a target still describing the old dimensions would be
silently wrong.

The tests pin this down rather than checking that something happened: a
0-degree rotation must return the masks unchanged, and a 90-degree rotation must
equal `masks$transpose(-1, -2)$flip(-2)` exactly, which is only true if no
interpolation occurred.

### 8. Add `ops_box_iou_rotated()`

[mlverse/torchvisionlib#34](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvisionlib/pull/34) ·
merged 17 August 2026 · +801 -1 across 23 files ·
fixes [#31](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvisionlib/issues/31)

Pairwise IoU between two sets of rotated boxes on CPU, returning an `N × M`
float32 matrix.

Three input formats are accepted: `cxcywhr` (centre, width, height, angle in
degrees), `xywhr` (top-left corner instead of centre), and `xyxyxyxy` (the four
corners directly). Conversion to `cxcywhr` happens in R, so the C++ kernel has
one representation to handle.

Rotated IoU is a genuinely different computation from the axis-aligned kind,
not a variation on `ops_nms()`. Two axis-aligned rectangles intersect in a
rectangle you can get from four `min`/`max` operations. Two rotated rectangles
intersect in a convex polygon of up to eight vertices, so the kernel has to clip
one box against the other and compute the area of the result. Having already
been through the export plumbing for the deformable attention op made the
non-kernel half of this PR much faster to write.

## Open pull requests

### `item_transform_resize()`

[mlverse/torchvision#380](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/380) ·
opened 9 August 2026 · +363 across 13 files ·
closes [#362](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/362) ·
**changes requested**

Resizing for detection items and datasets and for segmentation items and
datasets. Boxes are rescaled by the factors actually applied to the image
rather than the ones requested, which differ whenever aspect ratio is preserved
or rounding moves the output by a pixel. Masks resize with nearest-neighbour
sampling, for the same reason they do under rotation.

### `item_transform_random_resize_crop()`

[mlverse/torchvision#386](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/386) ·
opened 11 August 2026 · +556 -3 across 9 files ·
closes [#361](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/361) ·
**changes requested**

Random resized crop across all four item kinds: object detection item and
dataset, semantic segmentation item and dataset. The random parameters are
drawn once per item so that image and target receive the same crop, which is
the whole difficulty with random augmentation at the item level. Includes a fix
keeping the central-crop fallback inside the image bounds when the sampler fails
to find a valid crop.

### `item_transform_random_affine()`

[mlverse/torchvision#390](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/390) ·
opened 14 August 2026 · +458 -48 across 9 files ·
closes [#354](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/354) ·
**awaiting review**

Random affine for detection items, segmentation items and their datasets,
drawing rotation, translation, scale and shear once per item so image and
target stay aligned.

It also fixes a pre-existing bug in `transform_random_affine()`. Given a bare
number for `shear`, the function widened `degrees` into a range instead of
`shear`, leaving the shear range incomplete and making sampling fail. The bug
was invisible until something called the function with a scalar `shear`, which
is what the new item-level transform does.

### `object_detection_dataset` and `object_detection_target` S3 classes

[mlverse/torchvision#391](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/pull/391) ·
opened 19 August 2026 · +174 -26 across 21 files ·
closes [#364](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/issues/364) ·
**awaiting review**

A structural change rather than a new feature, and the natural conclusion of the
`item_transform_` work. Detection datasets now carry an
`object_detection_dataset` class and their item target `y` an
`object_detection_target` class, so target transforms dispatch on class instead
of inspecting which fields the target happens to have. Field inspection worked
while there was one kind of detection target, and stops working as soon as
there are two. Touches the COCO and Pascal VOC datasets and the six RF100
collections.
